title: The Rejected Shepherd and Thirty Pieces of Silver
summary: After a short lament over the fall of Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks, the prophet is commanded to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter, whose owners sell them without pity. He takes two staffs, Favor and Union, removes three shepherds, and then, weary of a flock that detests him, gives them up. When he asks for his wages they pay him thirty pieces of silver, which God tells him to throw to the potter in the house of the LORD. He breaks both staffs and is told to play the part of a worthless shepherd, on whom a final woe is pronounced.
story: Chapter 10 promised that God would care for his flock, judge the bad shepherds, and gather his scattered people. Chapter 11 is its dark counterpart: the flock rejects the shepherd God gives them. The hopeful movement of chapters 9 and 10 halts, and the chapter ends the first oracle collection (chapters 9 to 11) on a note of judgment. The second collection (chapters 12 to 14) will pick up the thread of a struck shepherd (13:7) and a pierced one (12:10), and move through grief and cleansing to final restoration. Many interpreters regard this chapter as one of the hardest in the Old Testament, and its details have been read in many ways.
historical:
The chapter gives no date, no names of rulers, and no clear historical markers, which is why its setting is so debated. The three shepherds removed in one month (verse 8) have been identified with dozens of candidates: kings of Israel from the eighth century, Persian kings, high priests of the Persian or Greek periods, or classes of leaders (kings, priests, and prophets). None of these identifications has won general agreement, and it is likely the chapter works as a symbolic drama rather than a coded history. The breaking of the staff called Union, which ends the brotherhood between Judah and Israel (verse 14), is often connected with the long split between Jerusalem and the people of the former northern kingdom, which hardened into the division between Jews and Samaritans in the Persian and Greek periods, though the date and course of that split are themselves debated.

The opening lament (verses 1-3) names real places known for their grandeur: the cedars of Lebanon, the great timber of the ancient Near East, the oaks of Bashan in the fertile highlands east of the Sea of Galilee, and the thickets along the Jordan where lions lived. Their fall pictures the fall of proud rulers.
cultural:
Shepherding was a hired trade as well as a family one. A shepherd might be employed by the owner of a flock and paid wages, and he answered to the owner for losses (Genesis 31:38-41). The staffs a shepherd carried were his basic tools, one for guiding and defending, sometimes paired with a heavier club (Psalm 23:4 names a rod and a staff). Naming them and breaking them was a symbolic act, like the sign-acts of Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

Thirty shekels of silver was the compensation the law required when an ox gored a slave to death (Exodus 21:32), so it may have been a set price for a slave; it is hard to say whether readers would have heard it as an insult, but verse 13 treats it with irony: this magnificent price at which they valued me. The potter worked in or near the temple, supplying vessels for its service; some scholars point out that Hebrew potter (yotser) is close to the word for treasury (otsar), and the ancient Syriac translation reads throw it into the treasury. Either way, the payment ends up in the house of the LORD, rejected like a worthless thing.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-3 are a short taunt song or lament in poetry. Verses 4-14, the heart of the chapter, are a prophetic sign-act told in the first person in prose: the prophet receives a command, performs it, and reports the result. Verses 15-17 are a second, shorter sign-act, playing a foolish shepherd, ending in a poetic woe. The narrative is built around the two staffs, named Favor (or Pleasantness) and Union (or Bonds), which are taken up in verse 7 and broken one after the other in verses 10 and 14, with the scene of the wages placed between the two breakings. The structure turns the chapter into a story of a covenant broken from both sides: the people reject the shepherd, and the shepherd withdraws.

outline.t: Lament over the fallen cedars and wailing shepherds
The command: shepherd the flock marked for slaughter
Two staffs, three shepherds removed, Favor broken
Thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter; Union broken
The foolish shepherd and the woe upon him

doctrines.note: When the flock detests its shepherd and values him at a slave's price, God withdraws his care and breaks the covenant bonds of favor and unity. Judgment here is God giving people what they have chosen: a shepherd who will devour rather than heal.

The chapter shows sin at work in leaders and people alike: owners who sell the flock and thank God for their profit, shepherds without pity, and a flock that despises the one sent to care for it. Rejecting God's shepherd is a rejection of God himself, since the LORD says it was at this price they valued me.

The chapter portrays a shepherd sent by God, rejected by the people, and valued at thirty pieces of silver. The New Testament sees this pattern fulfilled in Jesus, the good shepherd whom his people rejected.

words.note: Raah, to shepherd or pasture. The word runs through the whole chapter, as verb and as noun, applied to the prophet, the worthless shepherds, and the future foolish shepherd. It links this chapter to the shepherd themes of chapters 10 and 13 and to Ezekiel 34.
Noam, pleasantness, favor, or beauty. The first staff is named with it, standing for God's gracious protection of his flock against the nations. Breaking it in verse 10 revokes that protection.

Chovlim, bonds or union, from a word for cords that tie. The second staff stands for the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. Breaking it in verse 14 undoes the hope of reunion that chapter 10 had promised.

Yatsar, to form or shape; as a participle, a potter, one who forms clay. God commands the prophet to throw the thirty pieces of silver to the potter in the house of the LORD. The same imagery of the potter appears in Jeremiah 18 and 19, which helps explain why Matthew links this passage with Jeremiah.

christ: Matthew tells how Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14-15), then threw the money into the temple in remorse, and how the chief priests, unwilling to put blood money in the treasury, used it to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners (Matthew 27:3-10). Matthew sees this as fulfilling what was spoken through the prophet, and the wording closely follows Zechariah 11:12-13 blended with themes from Jeremiah. The parallel is striking: a shepherd sent by God is valued at a slave's price, and the money is thrown into the house of the LORD and ends with a potter. More broadly, the whole chapter anticipates the Gospels' account of a shepherd rejected by his own flock and its leaders, and of the flock left to the mercy of false shepherds. Jesus called himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and he wept over Jerusalem for not recognizing the time of its visitation (Luke 19:41-44).

hard.q: Why does Matthew attribute a quotation from Zechariah to Jeremiah?
hard.a: Matthew 27:9 introduces the fulfillment with the words spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, but the thirty pieces of silver and the throwing of money to the potter come from Zechariah 11. Several explanations are offered. Many scholars point out that Matthew's quotation is a composite: it draws its wording chiefly from Zechariah but its themes of a potter, a field bought, and a place of burial from Jeremiah (Jeremiah 18 to 19 and 32:6-15), and Matthew names the more prominent prophet, as Mark 1:2-3 names Isaiah for a quotation that blends Malachi and Isaiah. Others suggest that Jeremiah stood first in some ancient arrangements of the prophetic scrolls and could stand for the whole collection. A few think it was an early copying error, and some ancient manuscripts of Matthew read Zechariah or omit the name, though most read Jeremiah. The composite explanation is the most widely held and fits Matthew's practice elsewhere of weaving several Scriptures together.

questions: The flock detested the shepherd sent to care for them. Why do people sometimes reject the very care they most need?
The sellers of the flock thanked God for making them rich. How can religious language cover over injustice?
The shepherd was valued at a slave's price. What does it mean to you that Jesus was willing to be valued so cheaply?
